title: GOD ASKED, “WHOM SHALL I SEND?” ONE MAN ANSWERED BEFORE HE EVEN KNEW WHERE GOD WOULD SEND HIM.
paragraphs:
GOD ASKED, “WHOM SHALL I SEND?” ONE MAN ANSWERED BEFORE HE EVEN KNEW WHERE GOD WOULD SEND HIM.
Isaiah did not ask where. He did not ask how difficult it would be. He did not ask whether people would listen. He simply said, “Here I am. Send me.” But what happened immediately before those words changes everything about what surrender really means.
There are prayers we whisper because we want God to change our circumstances.
And then there are prayers that give God permission to change us.
Because surrender means handing Him the blank page before you know what He intends to write on it.
Isaiah prayed one of those prayers.
But perhaps you have heard his famous words so many times that they no longer frighten you.
Words printed across shirts, journals, church banners, and social media graphics.
But put Isaiah 6:8 back where Scripture placed it, and suddenly those words stop sounding decorative.
Because Isaiah did not receive an itinerary first.
God did not show him the audience.
God did not promise him applause.
God did not tell him that obedience would make him popular.
And surrendered before knowing what his yes would cost.
The Hebrew preserves the moment with breathtaking simplicity:
וָאֶשְׁמַע אֶת־קוֹל אֲדֹנָי אֹמֵר אֶת־מִי אֶשְׁלַח וּמִי יֵלֶךְ־לָנוּ וָאֹמַר הִנְנִי שְׁלָחֵנִי
Va’eshma et-qol Adonai omer, et-mi eshlah, umi yelekh-lanu? Va’omar: hinnēnî, šəlāḥēnî.
“I heard the voice of the Lord saying, ‘Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?’ Then I said, ‘Here am I; send me.’”
“What exactly do You want me to do?”
But there is something many of us miss when we rush straight to verse 8.
Isaiah did not begin the chapter saying, “Send me.”
Before there was commission, there was conviction.
Before there was mission, there was cleansing.
Before Isaiah volunteered his mouth for God, Isaiah became painfully aware that his mouth was unclean.
Isaiah sees the Lord “high and lifted up.”
And Isaiah does not look upon the holiness of God and congratulate himself for being spiritual enough to witness it.
The closer he comes to the holiness of God, the less impressive his own righteousness appears.
And perhaps that is where this story becomes yours.
Because it is possible to spend years around Christian things without truly seeing yourself before a holy God.
You can defend biblical truth online.
You can tell everybody else what they need to repent of…
while quietly protecting the one room inside your own heart where you do not want Jesus turning on the light.
And suddenly the excuses sound different.
The resentment toward your spouse looks different.
The dishonest business decision looks different.
The unforgiveness you renamed “boundaries” looks different.
The gossip you renamed “concern” looks different.
The spiritual laziness you renamed “being busy” looks different.
The compromise you promised yourself you could control looks different.
A sinful human being standing before unbearable holiness with absolutely nothing impressive enough to make himself clean.
But then something moves through the smoke.
A seraph flies toward Isaiah carrying a burning coal taken from the altar.
The coal touches the very place Isaiah confessed as unclean.
And Isaiah is told that his guilt has been taken away and his sin atoned for.
Isaiah did not repair his impurity and then approach God with an improved résumé.
Grace came to the place of his uncleanness.
That is why Isaiah 6 is more than a motivational speech about volunteering.
It reveals a biblical pattern that reaches its ultimate fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
Our sin must actually be dealt with.
And what Isaiah experiences symbolically through the altar points our eyes toward the greater reality proclaimed throughout the Gospel: sinners cannot save themselves.
And God did not leave humanity searching for one.
The sinless Son of God entered our fallen world, lived the righteousness we could never manufacture, gave Himself for sinners at the cross, was buried, and rose again.
The Gospel is not God pretending your sin never mattered.
The Gospel is that your sin mattered so terribly that redemption required a cost you could never pay—and Jesus willingly bore the judgment sinners deserved.
At Calvary, scandal collided with grace.
And because Jesus rewrites everything, the person who comes to Him in repentance and faith does not have to remain imprisoned by the chapter that once defined them.
The adulterer does not have to die merely “the adulterer.”
The addict does not have to remain merely “the addict.”
The liar does not have to remain “the liar.”
The bitter believer does not have to remain bitter.
The ashamed woman does not have to spend the rest of her life hiding.
The broken man does not have to pretend he was never broken.
Grace does not call evil good.
Grace forgives the guilty and begins transforming the forgiven.
And now we finally understand why Isaiah could say:
The man answering God in verse 8 is the man who cried “Woe is me” in verse 5.
That changes the entire meaning of Christian service.
We do not surrender so God will forgive us.
In Christ, we surrender because His grace has captured us.
We do not serve to purchase redemption.
We serve because redemption cannot leave a surrendered heart untouched.
And here comes the uncomfortable part.
Isaiah said yes before hearing the assignment.
His ministry would not be an easy road of instant visible success.
He would speak to people resistant to the message.
That may be one of the most painfully human questions in the chapter.
How long do I keep praying for this child?
How long do I remain faithful when nobody notices?
How long do I fight this temptation?
How long do I keep serving when I feel invisible?
How long do I speak truth when people would rather hear something comfortable?
How long do I trust You when nothing looks the way I thought obedience would look?
Somewhere along the way, many of us absorbed a version of Christianity in which obedience was supposed to produce immediate visible rewards.
Follow God and everything falls into place.
Serve faithfully and people appreciate you.
Pray faithfully and the answer arrives according to schedule.
But Isaiah's calling destroys that illusion.
Sometimes obedience sends you directly into difficulty.
Sometimes you speak and people reject you.
Sometimes you obey God without getting the outcome you hoped obedience would produce.
Sometimes your assignment is not to be impressive.
It is simply to be faithful.
That is why hinnēnî is so costly.
Not merely the parts of my life I am comfortable giving You.
And maybe that is the sentence God has been waiting to hear from you.
Not because God lacks power without you.
God is not pacing heaven desperately hoping somebody will rescue His plans.
The sovereign Lord who filled Isaiah's vision does not need human beings in the way human beings need Him.
The wonder is that He calls people at all.
He allows redeemed sinners to participate in His purposes.
The God before whom seraphim cover themselves chooses to send forgiven human beings into the world carrying His truth.
And centuries after Isaiah, Jesus would speak again about sending.
After His resurrection, Christ told His disciples that as the Father had sent Him, He was sending them.
The risen Christ would commission His followers to make disciples of the nations.
Christianity was never intended to terminate with us.
Someone carried the Gospel until it reached you.
Someone opened a Bible at a kitchen table.
Someone shared the truth when staying silent would have been easier.
Now the question travels across centuries and lands uncomfortably close to your own heart.
Perhaps you have been waiting for God to give you the whole map before you surrender.
God, show me exactly what happens, and then I will trust You.
Show me what I will earn.
Show me whether they will accept me.
Show me whether I will get hurt.
Isaiah's answer came before the explanation.
And before you turn that sentence into an emotional promise, remember where Isaiah's surrender began.
So perhaps your first hinnēnî today is not “Send me to another country.”
Jesus, here is the sin I have been hiding.
Here is the relationship I know dishonors You.
Here is the grudge I keep feeding.
Here is the secret version of me nobody at church knows exists.
And when Christ forgives you, do not mistake grace for permission to return comfortably to the chains from which He came to rescue you.
Grace teaches surrendered people to say yes.
Maybe your “send me” means finally sharing the Gospel with your family.
Maybe it means opening your home.
Maybe it means discipling your children instead of outsourcing their spiritual formation.
Maybe it means returning to church after shame convinced you to disappear.
Maybe it means refusing the compromise everybody else calls normal.
Maybe it means using your business, your voice, your resources, your social media, your influence, your suffering, your testimony, or your remaining years for the glory of Jesus Christ.
You may never stand behind a pulpit.
You may never have a platform.
Your name may never become famous.
And there is a world of difference.
There are other believers reading who need to discover that they are not fighting alone.
Your honesty may become somebody else's permission to finally ask for prayer.
Not merely because an algorithm rewards sharing.
Send this privately to the person you cannot stop thinking about while reading.
Because one day the cost of your own “yes” may become heavier than the emotion you feel right now, and you may need to come back and remember:
Isaiah did not know everything when he volunteered.
He knew the One calling him.
Not because paying for something earns God's favor.
Christ purchased salvation; we cannot buy it.
But supporting Gospel-centered work can be one practical way of helping biblical encouragement, discipleship resources, and Gospel proclamation continue reaching people.
Not as a transaction with God.
Not because sharing a post somehow makes you righteous.
Share because the Gospel is worth carrying.
Support faithful Christian work because generosity can serve the spread of truth.
Maybe heaven's question is closer than you thought.
Maybe God has already placed someone within reach of your testimony.
Maybe somebody needs the Gospel you have been too afraid to share.
Maybe your children need to see what surrendered Christianity actually looks like.
Maybe the person God intends to use is not a more talented person, a less wounded person, a more educated person, or a person with a cleaner history.
Maybe grace has brought you all the way to this sentence.
You do not need to know every mile of the road before entrusting yourself to the One who already knows where it ends.
And perhaps that is the line worth carrying with you long after this article disappears from your screen:
The man who once cried, “Woe is me,” became the man who could say, “Send me”—because grace touched the very place where shame told him he was unusable.
